summary: This note is the Oxford Academic landing page for a 1976 Public Opinion Quarterly article by James M. Fields and Howard Schuman, titled "Public Beliefs About the Beliefs of the Public". The article examines how people perceive the opinions of others, using data from three sample surveys of metropolitan Detroit. The abstract reports substantial inaccuracy in such perceptions and identifies three tendencies: "looking glass perceptions," "conservative bias," and limited response to reality constraints. The rest of the page is navigation, access, and citation boilerplate; the full text is only available as a PDF.
one_line: A 1976 Public Opinion Quarterly study by Fields and Schuman on how people misperceive others' opinions, based on Detroit surveys.
key_facts: The article "Public Beliefs About the Beliefs of the Public" was written by James M. Fields and Howard Schuman.
It was published in Public Opinion Quarterly, Volume 40, Issue 4, Winter 1976, pages 427–448.
The article was published on 01 January 1976 and has DOI 10.1086/268330.
The perceptions studied were examined using data from three sample surveys of metropolitan Detroit.
The abstract states that a great deal of inaccuracy in perception of others' opinions is evident.
One identified pattern is "looking glass perceptions," the general propensity to believe that others' opinions are the same as one's own.
A second identified pattern is "conservative bias," the belief that the population is more conservative on racial issues than it actually is.
A third identified pattern is limited response to reality constraints.
The authors conclude that perceptions of public beliefs and attitudes are personally and socially constructed to a much larger degree than is often assumed.
The article is categorized as a research article and is only available as a PDF.
The page reports 262 total citations on Dimensions and 353 views.
The journal is published by the American Association for Public Opinion Research and its online ISSN is 1537-5331.
